title: Realtime Trust & Cost Manifesto
body:
One-pager intent

This note reframes Redwood’s core mission around two promises that buyers actually act on: realtime trust (predictable latency + graceful degradation) and session-level cost control (clear, actionable economics for feature teams). Goal: give GTM succinct hooks and engineer-friendly proof points for sales decks, product pages, and launch briefs.

Mission (short)
Make inference predictable at scale so engineering teams can ship latency-sensitive experiences without trading away cost discipline or reliability.

Thesis (compact)
As LLMs move from experiments to customer-facing features, winning teams assume responsibility for user-level experience guarantees — not just model accuracy. That means: latency and availability guarantees per session, transparent per-session economics, and simple operational primitives to reason about regressions. Vendors who deliver a developer-first runtime plus clear cost controls will be treated as infrastructure, not commodities.

Problem we solve (plain)
- Teams building real-time experiences (chat, agents, assistive UIs) face unpredictable tail latency and opaque token economics.
- Workflows break in production when models, sequence lengths, or traffic patterns change; debugging is slow and costly.
- Platform teams waste cycles building routing/fallback, cost controls, and observability instead of product features.

Redwood’s one-line promise
Predictable realtime inference with session-aware cost controls — so you can ship delightful, reliable features and know exactly what they cost.

Why this angle (evidence)
- Dev-first buyers repeatedly ask for SLA-like guarantees they can reason about (p99 latency, session availability, cost per session) in plain terms.
- Many competitors optimize single levers (model access, lowest cost, or simplicity) but don’t combine latency SLO tooling, fallbacks, and cost telemetry at the session level.
- Customers value pragmatic fallbacks (model downgrade paths, region reroute, cached prefix reuse) over hyped model quality claims when user experience is on the line.

Core differentiators (short bullets)
- Session-level SLOs: route, observe, and alert on session p95/p99 latency and availability rather than only token rates.
- Cost-as-metrics: per-session cost breakdowns (model, tokens, compute delta) exposed in console + API for chargeback and optimization.
- Graceful hybrid fallbacks: automated downgrade policies that preserve semantics while saving cost and preserving uptime.
- Developer ergonomics: same API and rollout controls across hosted/dedicated/private with simple model pinning and canary rules.
- Runtime-first economics: kernel selection + batching that optimize for common realtime distributions (short interactive requests with occasional long tails).

Proof points & signals we can use in GTM
- Benchmarks: p99 latency under mixed short/long workloads with our hybrid fallback enabled (publish numbers by model family + typical seq distributions).
- Case study: a customer reduced median session cost by X% while improving p99 by Y ms after adopting caching + fallback rules. (placeholder: fill with actual customer names when available).
- Observable playbook: reproducible steps to diagnose session regressions (trace → route decision → cache miss → fallback).

Target audiences and tailored hooks
- Platform teams: "Give teams safe defaults and chargeback-ready cost signals to decentralize LLM features."
- Product engineering: "Ship latency-sensitive UX without reimplementing inference ops; use rollouts & fallbacks."
- CTO/Infrastructure: "Consolidate inference footprint across hosted/dedicated/private with consistent SLOs and predictable economics."

Key messaging snippets (compact copy for decks)
- Headline: Predictable realtime inference + transparent cost per session.
- Subhead: A runtime and control plane that treats inference as an experience — not a model slot.
- One-liner for console: See cost and latency per session, enforce SLOs, and roll out safer fallbacks.

Competitive framing (how to position vs. three archetypes)
- Versus model-access-first APIs: emphasize operational primitives and session economics — not just access.
- Versus low-cost self-hosted runtimes: emphasize the control plane, canary/fallback automation, observability, and enterprise packaging.
- Versus cloud managed endpoints: emphasize unified interface across deployment modes and developer ergonomics for multi-tenant product teams.

Suggested collateral and experiments (quick list)
- Small playbook doc: "How to think about session SLOs" (customer-facing checklist + templates).
- Benchmark sheet: p50/p95/p99 numbers across sample workloads and models with and without fallback.
- Short demo: show a chat UI where a long request triggers fallback and the console shows per-session cost drop.

Rollout guidance for GTM materials
- Start internal: equip AE and SE with 2-slide kernel of this narrative + expected proof points.
- Replace technical wording in outward docs with "session" language (session SLAs, session cost).
- Integrate into pricing pages: show exemplar session pricing scenarios and cost drivers.

Open questions / followups (do this before public push)
- Agree on standard session definitions (how to count session cost across restarts / agent calls).
- Finalize benchmark templates and run consistency tests across regions.
- Identify 2 customer pilots for a public case study focused on realtime UX.

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep this short — GTM needs quick, repeatable lines.
- Sync with product on API primitives for session-level telemetry UX.
- Capture a simple vignette for sales: "How Redwood kept customer X’s 99th percentile chat latency under 350ms during holiday traffic."

End.
